children.name: Hirundo
children.description: Barn swallows — the most familiar swallows on Earth and one of the most widespread birds in the world. The barn swallow (ladusvala) is a summer visitor of immense cultural significance in Sweden: its arrival in late April or early May is celebrated as a defining moment of the Nordic year. Swallows have lived alongside humans for millennia, nesting in barns, stables, and buildings and feeding on the insects attracted to livestock — a mutualistic relationship that has made them simultaneously dependent on and beloved by farming communities. Swallows are aerial masters, capable of sustained flight speeds exceeding 70 km/h and catching all their food on the wing. They are long-distance migrants, wintering in sub-Saharan Africa and covering up to 10,000 km each way.

children.name: Hirundo rustica
children.description: The barn swallow is the most widespread species of swallow in the world, occurring on all continents, with vagrants reported even in Antarctica. It is a distinctive passerine bird with blue upperparts and a long, deeply forked tail. In Anglophone Europe, it is just called the swallow; in northern Europe, it is the only member of family Hirundinidae called a "swallow" rather than a "martin".

children.name: Hirundo lucida
children.description:
The red-chested swallow (Hirundo lucida) is a small non-migratory passerine bird found in West Africa, the Congo Basin and Ethiopia. It has a long, deeply forked tail and curved, pointed wings.
It was formerly considered a subspecies of the closely resembling barn swallow. However, the adult red-chested swallow differs in being slightly smaller than its migratory relative, in addition to having a narrower blue breast band and shorter tail streamers. Juveniles are more comparable to barn swallow chicks.

children.name: Hirundo angolensis
children.description: The Angola swallow (Hirundo angolensis) is a species of swallow that is native to the Afrotropics.

children.name: Hirundo tahitica
children.description: The Tahiti swallow (Hirundo tahitica) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Hirundo neoxena
children.description: The welcome swallow (Hirundo neoxena) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae that is native to Australia and nearby islands.

children.name: Hirundo nigrorufa
children.description: The black-and-rufous swallow (Hirundo nigrorufa) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Hirundo smithii
children.description: The wire-tailed swallow (Hirundo smithii) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family. It has two subspecies: H. S. Smithii, which occurs throughout Africa, and H. S. Filifera, which is found in southern and southeastern Asia. It is mainly resident, but populations in Pakistan and northern India migrate further south in winter. The genus name Hirundo is the Latin word for swallow. The species name smithii commemorates Christen Smith, a Norwegian botanist and geologist.

children.name: Hirundo aethiopica
children.description: The Ethiopian swallow (Hirundo aethiopica) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Hirundo nigrita
children.description: The white-bibbed swallow (Hirundo nigrita), also known as the white-throated blue swallow, is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae. It is widespread across the African tropical rainforest (Dahomey Gap also).

children.name: Hirundo dimidiata
children.description: The pearl-breasted swallow (Hirundo dimidiata) is a small swallow.

children.name: Hirundo leucosoma
children.description: The pied-winged swallow (Hirundo leucosoma) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae. It has distinctive steel-blue upperparts with white wing patches. It is native to parts of West Africa.

children.name: Hirundo megaensis
children.description: The white-tailed swallow (Hirundo megaensis) is a small swallow belonging to the family Hirundinidae and is endemic to Oromia, Ethiopia. It is commonly referred to as "Benson's swallow" after the ornithologist Constantine Walter Benson, who described the species. This small bird is classified as a vulnerable species by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), as there is a progressive declination of the species which now consists of less than 10,000 adult individuals worldwide. It has a surprisingly small range for a swallow, as it is wholly dependent on a cooler "bubble" surrounding its small range, likely for proper breeding success. It is one of the most threatened bird species by climate change and a massive range reduction is projected in the future.

children.name: Cecropis
children.description: Striated and rufous swallows — a genus of Old World swallows split from Hirundo, characterized by streaked or rufous underparts and often prominent rufous rumps. They are found across Africa and Asia, with one species extending to Europe and another resident in Australia. Several are associated with rocky gorges and cliffs, while others nest in buildings and under bridges.

children.name: Cecropis daurica
children.description:
The eastern red-rumped swallow (Cecropis daurica) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae. It is found in open, often hilly, areas with clearings and cultivation across Southeast Asia to north-eastern India and Taiwan.
The European red-rumped swallow and the African red-rumped swallow were formerly considered as subspecies of the eastern red-rumped swallow.

children.name: Cecropis striolata
children.description:
The eastern red-rumped swallow (Cecropis daurica) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae. It is found in open, often hilly, areas with clearings and cultivation across Southeast Asia to north-eastern India and Taiwan.
The European red-rumped swallow and the African red-rumped swallow were formerly considered as subspecies of the eastern red-rumped swallow.

children.name: Cecropis badia
children.description: The rufous-bellied swallow (Cecropis badia) is a species of swallow that breeds on the Malay Peninsula. It has faintly streaked deep rufous underparts, and an unstreaked rump. It is usually raised to species status from its closest relative, the striated swallow.

children.name: Cecropis abyssinica
children.description: The lesser striped swallow (Cecropis abyssinica) is a large swallow. It breeds in Sub-Saharan Africa from Sierra Leone and southern Sudan south into eastern South Africa. It is partially migratory with South African birds wintering further north. West African birds leave the north of the breeding range in the dry season.

children.name: Cecropis senegalensis
children.description: The mosque swallow (Cecropis senegalensis) is a large species of swallow.

children.name: Cecropis cucullata
children.description: The greater striped swallow (Cecropis cucullata) is a large swallow that is native to Africa south of the equator.

children.name: Cecropis hyperythra
children.description: The Sri Lanka swallow (Cecropis hyperythra) is a resident breeder endemic to Sri Lanka. It is closely related to the red-rumped swallow, and was formerly considered a subspecies.

children.name: Cecropis domicella
children.description: The African red-rumped swallow (Cecropis melanocrissus) is small passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae. It is found in north tropical areas of Africa south of the Sahara.

children.name: Petrochelidon
children.description: Cliff swallows and allies — a genus of colonial swallows that build retort-shaped mud nests on cliff faces and man-made structures. The group spans North America, Africa, and Australia. The American cliff swallow is one of the most spectacular colonial birds in North America, with colonies sometimes numbering tens of thousands of nests under highway overpasses.

children.name: Petrochelidon pyrrhonota
children.description: The cliff swallow or American cliff swallow (Petrochelidon pyrrhonota) is a member of the passerine bird family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Petrochelidon fulva
children.description: The cave swallow (Petrochelidon fulva) is a medium-sized, squarish-tailed swallow belonging to the same genus as the more familiar and widespread cliff swallow of North America.

children.name: Petrochelidon rufigula
children.description: The red-throated cliff swallow (Petrochelidon rufigula), also known as the red-throated swallow, is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae. It is found in Angola, Republic of the Congo, DRC, Gabon, and Zambia.

children.name: Petrochelidon preussi
children.description: Preuss's cliff swallow (Petrochelidon preussi), also known as Preuss's swallow, is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Petrochelidon perdita
children.description: The Red Sea cliff swallow (Petrochelidon perdita), also known as the Red Sea swallow, is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Petrochelidon nigricans
children.description: The tree martin (Petrochelidon nigricans) is a member of the swallow family of passerine birds.

children.name: Petrochelidon ariel
children.description: The fairy martin (Petrochelidon ariel) is a member of the swallow family of passerine birds which breeds in Australia.

children.name: Petrochelidon fluvicola
children.description: The streak-throated swallow or the Indian cliff swallow (Petrochelidon fluvicola) is a passerine bird, which includes a large number of other species including many swallows. It is native of South Asia where it is a breeder, year-round resident or winter visitor in the countries of Afghanistan, India, Nepal and Pakistan. It occurs as a vagrant in the Maldives, Sri Lanka, and the Middle East.

children.name: Petrochelidon frontalis
children.description: A colonial cliff swallow of the Himalayan foothills and hills of South and Southeast Asia, building enclosed mud nests on rocky cliff faces and under bridges. It is closely related to the streak-throated swallow and was long treated as its subspecies. The species has a more restricted distribution in the foothills of Nepal, Bangladesh, and adjacent Myanmar.

children.name: Petrochelidon rufocollaris
children.description: The chestnut-collared swallow (Petrochelidon rufocollaris) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins. It is found in Ecuador and Peru.

children.name: Petrochelidon spilodera
children.description:
The South African cliff swallow (Petrochelidon spilodera), also known as the South African swallow, is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae native southern Africa. It winters to the lower Congo Basin.
Nests are commonly built from mud under artificial structures such as huts and bridges. It is well known for its supposed ability to carry coconuts, although this claim has little to no credibility outside of the Monty Python fictional universe.

children.name: Delichon
children.description: House martins — compact, blue-black and white swallows that build dome-shaped mud nests attached to cliff faces and — most famously — under the eaves of houses. The common house martin (hussvala) is a familiar summer visitor to Swedish towns and villages, and established colonies under roof eaves can be decades old. House martins collect mud for nest construction from puddles and stream banks, sometimes travelling considerable distances from their nesting site. They are more colonial than barn swallows, often building nests immediately adjacent to one another. Despite their name and intimate association with human buildings, relatively little is known about their winter quarters in sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Delichon urbicum
children.description: The western house martin, sometimes called the common house martin, northern house martin or, particularly in Europe, just house martin, is a migratory passerine bird of the swallow family which breeds in Europe, north Africa and west-central Asia; and winters in sub-Saharan Africa and southwestern Asia. It feeds on insects which are caught in flight, and it migrates to climates where flying insects are plentiful. It has a blue head and upperparts, white rump and pure white underparts, and is found in both open country and near human habitation.

children.name: Delichon dasypus
children.description:
The Asian house martin (Delichon dasypus) is a migratory passerine bird of the swallow family Hirundinidae. It has mainly blue-black upperparts, other than its white rump, and has pale grey underparts. Its three subspecies breed in the Himalayas and in central and eastern Asia, and spend the winter lower in the mountains or in Southeast Asia. This species is locally abundant and is expanding northward in Siberia, so there are no concerns about its conservation status.
This martin breeds in colonies, building mud nests under an overhang on a vertical cliff or the wall of a building. Both sexes build the nest, incubate the three or four white eggs and feed the chicks. The Asian house martin feeds on small insects taken in flight, usually caught high in the air. The presence of terrestrial springtails and Lepidoptera larvae in its diet indicates that food is sometimes picked from the ground.

children.name: Delichon nipalense
children.description:
The Nepal house martin (Delichon nipalense) is a non-migratory passerine of the swallow family Hirundinidae. Its two subspecies breed in the Himalayas from northwestern India through Nepal to Myanmar, northern Vietnam, and just into China. It occurs in river valleys and rugged wooded mountain ridges at heights between altitude, where it nests in colonies beneath overhangs on vertical cliffs, laying three or four white eggs in an enclosed mud nest.
This martin has blue-black upperparts with a contrasting white rump, and white underparts. It resembles its close relatives, the Asian house martin and common house martin, but unlike those species it has a black throat and black undertail. It feeds in flocks with other swallows, catching flies and other insects in flight. It is subject to predation and parasites, but its status within its limited range appears secure.

children.name: Riparia
children.description: Sand martins — the smallest and brownest of Sweden's swallows, colonial nesters in sandy riverbanks, sand quarries, and sea cliffs. Each pair excavates a tunnel 30–90 cm deep in bare sand, ending in a nesting chamber — a feat of engineering for a bird weighing just 13 grams. Sand martin colonies can number thousands of pairs and create dramatic, buzzing spectacles when the birds return to their colony after feeding. They are among the earliest summer migrants to arrive in Sweden in spring, and their presence at a colony site can be assessed instantly by the dark rings of nest holes peppering the sand face.

children.name: Riparia riparia
children.description: The sand martin, also known as the collared sand martin or common sand martin, and in the Americas as the bank swallow, is a migratory passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae. It has a wide range in summer, embracing practically the whole Holarctic area, from Europe, across Asia to the Pacific Ocean, and throughout North America. It winters in eastern and southern Africa, southern Asia, and South America.

children.name: Riparia paludicola
children.description: The brown-throated martin, brown-throated sand martin or plain martin (Riparia paludicola) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family, Hirundinidae, that is widely distributed across Africa. It was formerly regarded as conspecific with the grey-throated martin (Riparia chinensis) and the Madagascar martin (Riparia cowani).

children.name: Riparia congica
children.description: The Congo martin or Congo sand martin (Riparia congica) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Riparia cincta
children.description: The banded martin or banded sand martin (Neophedina cincta) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae that is endemic to Africa.

children.name: Riparia diluta
children.description: The pale martin or pale sand martin (Riparia diluta) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Riparia chinensis
children.description:
The grey-throated martin or Asian plain martin (Riparia chinensis) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.
The grey-throated martin is found in open habitats such as farmland, grassland and savannah, usually near water. It is found from Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Indian subcontinent to southern China, Taiwan, and the northern Philippines. It was formerly considered a subspecies of the plain martin, since renamed the brown-throated martin.

children.name: Ptyonoprogne
children.description: Crag martins — robust, earth-coloured swallows of rocky mountains and gorges. The Eurasian crag martin nests on cliff faces and rocky outcrops, plastering a mud cup to vertical rock surfaces in locations completely inaccessible to terrestrial predators. They are resident year-round in southern Europe's mountain ranges, one of the few swallows that don't make long-distance migrations. In Sweden, crag martins are rare vagrants rather than breeding birds, occasionally seen along coastal cliffs in autumn. Their flight is more leisurely and gliding than other swallows, matching the thermal-soaring conditions of mountain environments.

children.name: Ptyonoprogne rupestris
children.description: The Eurasian crag martin or just crag martin (Ptyonoprogne rupestris) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Ptyonoprogne obsoleta
children.description:
The pale crag martin (Ptyonoprogne obsoleta) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family that is resident in Northern Africa and in Southwestern Asia, east to Pakistan. It breeds mainly in the mountains, but also at lower altitudes, especially in rocky areas and around towns. Unlike most swallows, it is often found far from water. It is long, with mainly brown plumage, paler-toned on the upper breast and underwing coverts, and with white "windows" on the spread tail in flight. The sexes are similar in appearance, but juveniles have pale fringes to the upperparts and flight feathers. It was formerly considered to be the northern subspecies of the rock martin of southern Africa, although it is smaller, paler, and whiter-throated than that species. The pale crag martin hunts along cliff faces for flying insects using a slow flight with much gliding. Its call is a soft twitter.
This martin builds a deep bowl nest on a sheltered horizontal surface, or a neat quarter-sphere against a vertical rock face or wall. The nest is constructed with mud pellets and lined with grass or feathers, and may be built on natural sites under cliff overhangs or on man-made structures such as buildings and bridges. It is often reused for subsequent broods or in later years. This species is often a solitary breeder, but small groups may breed close together in suitable locations. The two or three eggs of a typical clutch are white with brown and grey blotches, and are incubated by both adults for 16–19 days prior to hatching. Both parents then feed the chicks. Fledging takes another 22–24 days, although the young birds will return to the nest to roost for a few days after their first flight.

children.name: Ptyonoprogne fuligula
children.description:
The large rock martin (Ptyonoprogne fuligula), also known as the southern crag-martin, is a small passerine bird in the swallow family that is resident in southern Africa. It was formerly considered to be conspecific with the red-throated rock martin. It breeds mainly in the mountains, but also at lower altitudes, especially in rocky areas and around towns, and, unlike most swallows, it is often found far from water. It is long, with mainly brown plumage, paler-toned on the upper breast and underwing coverts, and with white "windows" on the spread tail in flight. The sexes are similar in appearance, but juveniles have pale fringes to the upperparts and flight feathers. The former northern subspecies are smaller, paler, and whiter-throated than southern African forms, and are now usually split as a separate species, the pale crag martin. The large rock martin hunts along cliff faces for flying insects using a slow flight with much gliding. Its call is a soft twitter.
The large rock martin builds a deep bowl nest on a sheltered horizontal surface, or a neat quarter-sphere against a vertical rock face or wall. The nest is constructed with mud pellets and lined with grass or feathers, and may be built on natural sites under cliff overhangs or on man-made structures such as buildings, dam walls, culverts and bridges. It is often reused for subsequent broods or in later years. The large rock martin is a solitary breeder, and is not gregarious, but small groups may breed close together in suitable locations. The two or three eggs of a typical clutch are white with brown and grey blotches, and are incubated by both adults for 16–19 days prior to hatching. Both parents then feed the chicks. Fledging takes another 22–24 days, but the young birds will return to the nest to roost for a few days after the first flight.

children.name: Ptyonoprogne concolor
children.description:
The dusky crag martin (Ptyonoprogne concolor) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family. It is about long with a broad body and wings, and a short square tail that has small white patches near the tips of most of its feathers. This martin has sooty-brown upperparts and slightly paler underparts. The two subspecies are resident breeding birds in South Asia from the Indian subcontinent to southwestern China and the northern parts of Thailand, Vietnam and Laos.
This martin nests under a cliff overhang or on a man-made structure, building a neat half-cup mud nest with a soft lining. Both adults incubate the two to four eggs and feed the chicks. This species does not form large breeding colonies, but it is more gregarious outside the breeding season. It feeds a wide variety of insects that are caught as the martin flies near to cliff faces. It may be hunted by large bats as well as birds of prey, but its extensive and expanding range and large population mean that there are no significant conservation concerns.

children.name: Pseudhirundo
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the grey-rumped swallow of sub-Saharan Africa. The grey-rumped swallow is an unusual African hirundine that was long associated with Riparia but differs in its grey rump and preference for forest edge habitats. It builds its nest in burrows in banks or old woodpecker holes in trees.

children.name: Pseudhirundo griseopyga
children.description:
The grey-rumped swallow (Pseudhirundo griseopyga) is a species of swallow. It is the only member of the genus Pseudhirundo.
It is found in Angola, Benin, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Republic of the Congo, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ivory Coast, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Kenya, Liberia, Malawi, Mali, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, Sierra Leone, South Africa, Sudan, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.

children.name: Psalidoprocne
children.description: Saw-wings — a genus of African swallows named for the serrated outer primary feathers of the males, a unique structural feature among birds. They inhabit forest, woodland, and edge habitats across sub-Saharan Africa. Saw-wings are often associated with forest streams and ravines, and their flight style is more fluttering and bat-like than that of open-country swallows.

children.name: Psalidoprocne albiceps
children.description:
The white-headed saw-wing (Psalidoprocne albiceps), also known as the white-headed rough-winged swallow is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae. It is found in Angola, Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Rwanda, South Sudan, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia.
This species has an extremely large range, and hence does not approach the thresholds for Vulnerable under the range size criterion (Extent of Occurrence 30% decline over ten years or three generations). The population size has not been quantified, but it is not believed to approach the thresholds for Vulnerable under the population size criterion (10% in ten years or three generations, or with a specified population structure). For these reasons the species is evaluated as Least Concern by the IUCN.

children.name: Psalidoprocne antinorii
children.description: The black saw-wing (Psalidoprocne pristoptera), also known as the blue saw-wing or black rough-winged swallow, is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Psalidoprocne fuliginosa
children.description:
The mountain saw-wing (Psalidoprocne fuliginosa), also known as the mountain rough-winged swallow or the Cameroon Mountain rough-winged swallow is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae.
It is native to the Mount Cameroon and Bioko montane forests. While it has been reported elsewhere in Central Africa (namely, the Cameroon line of Cameroon and Nigeria), it has never been confirmed.

children.name: Psalidoprocne holomelaena
children.description: A widespread, entirely black saw-wing found across east and southern Africa in montane forest and adjacent woodland. It is the most frequently observed saw-wing in much of eastern Africa. Both sexes are uniformly black, lacking the contrasting white head of some relatives.

children.name: Psalidoprocne nitens
children.description: The square-tailed saw-wing (Psalidoprocne nitens), also known as the square-tailed rough-winged swallow is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae. It is native to the African tropical rainforest.

children.name: Psalidoprocne orientalis
children.description: The black saw-wing (Psalidoprocne pristoptera), also known as the blue saw-wing or black rough-winged swallow, is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Psalidoprocne petiti
children.description: The black saw-wing (Psalidoprocne pristoptera), also known as the blue saw-wing or black rough-winged swallow, is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Psalidoprocne pristoptera
children.description: The black saw-wing (Psalidoprocne pristoptera), also known as the blue saw-wing or black rough-winged swallow, is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Psalidoprocne oleaginea
children.description: The black saw-wing (Psalidoprocne pristoptera), also known as the blue saw-wing or black rough-winged swallow, is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Phedina
children.description: A small genus of African martins with streaked underparts, found in Madagascar and central Africa. They inhabit open country near water and forest clearings, and are among the less well-studied hirundines. The Mascarene martin is a migratory species that moves between breeding and wintering areas within the Indian Ocean region.

children.name: Phedina borbonica
children.description: The Mascarene martin or Mascarene swallow is a passerine bird in the swallow family that breeds in Madagascar and in the Mascarene Islands. The nominate subspecies occurs on Mauritius and Réunion and has never been found away from the Mascarene Islands, but the smaller Madagascan subspecies, P. madagascariensis, is migratory and has been recorded wintering in East Africa or wandering to other Indian Ocean islands.

children.name: Progne
children.description: Purple martins and their allies — the largest swallows in the Americas, with glossy blue-black plumage in males and more dusky or brown females. Progne martins are strongly associated with human-provided nest boxes and gourds in North America, where the purple martin has become almost entirely dependent on man-made nest structures east of the Rockies. South American species tend to inhabit open savanna and forest edge, often nesting in palm cavities.

children.name: Progne subis
children.description: The purple martin (Progne subis) is a passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Progne cryptoleuca
children.description: The Cuban martin (Progne cryptoleuca) is a large swallow endemic to Cuba.

children.name: Progne dominicensis
children.description: | range_map = Progne dominicensis map.svg.

children.name: Progne elegans
children.description: The southern martin (Progne elegans) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Progne chalybea
children.description: The grey-breasted martin (Progne chalybea) is a large swallow from Central and South America.

children.name: Progne modesta
children.description: The Galapagos martin (Progne modesta) is an Endangered species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins. It is endemic to the Galápagos Islands.

children.name: Progne murphyi
children.description: The Peruvian martin (Progne murphyi) is a Near Threatened species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Progne tapera
children.description: The brown-chested martin (Progne tapera) is a species of passerine bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins. It is found regularly in Panama and every mainland South American country except Chile. It has been documented as a vagrant in Aruba and Chile and there are unconfirmed reports from the Falkland Islands. It is a casual visitor to Costa Rica and has been recorded in Florida, Massachusetts, and New Jersey.

children.name: Progne sinaloae
children.description: The Sinaloa martin (Progne sinaloae) is a Vulnerable species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Tachycineta
children.description: A New World genus of iridescent green, blue, or violet swallows, including the tree swallow — one of the most studied birds in the world due to its enthusiastic adoption of nest boxes. Tachycineta swallows range from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, with several island endemics in the Caribbean. Their tree swallow populations have served as a model for understanding the effects of climate change on avian breeding phenology.

children.name: Tachycineta bicolor
children.description: The tree swallow (Tachycineta bicolor) is a migratory bird of the family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Tachycineta thalassina
children.description: The violet-green swallow (Tachycineta thalassina) is a small North American passerine bird in the swallow family. These aerial insectivores are distributed along the west coast from Alaska to Mexico, extending as far east as Montana and Texas. With an appearance very similar to the tree swallow, these individuals can be identified by the white rump side-patches that appear to separate their green back and purple tail. Violet-green swallows are secondary cavity nesters, found in a number of habitats including deciduous and coniferous forest. In addition to nesting in tree holes within these habitats, they are also widely observed nesting in the cracks of large cliffs.

children.name: Tachycineta cyaneoviridis
children.description: The Bahama swallow (Tachycineta cyaneoviridis) is an endangered swallow endemic to The Bahamas.

children.name: Tachycineta stolzmanni
children.description: The Tumbes swallow (Tachycineta stolzmanni) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Tachycineta albiventer
children.description: The white-winged swallow (Tachycineta albiventer) is a resident breeding swallow in tropical South America found in Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, Trinidad, and Argentina. It is not found west of the Andes. This swallow is largely non-migratory.

children.name: Tachycineta meyeni
children.description: The Chilean swallow (Tachycineta leucopyga) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Tachycineta leucorrhoa
children.description:
The white-rumped swallow (Tachycineta leucorrhoa) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae. First described and given its binomial name by French ornithologist Louis Pierre Vieillot in 1817, it was for many years considered a subspecies of the Chilean swallow. The species is monotypic with no known population variations. It has a white streak, or streak above its lores (the region between a bird's eye and nostrils), which can be used to differentiate it from the Chilean swallow. The lores, ear coverts, tail, and wings are black, with white tips on the inner secondaries, tertials, and greater coverts of the wings. The rest of the are a glossy blue. Its underparts and underwing-coverts are white, in addition to the rump, as the name suggests. The sexes are similar, and the juvenile is duller and browner with a dusky breast.
This species usually builds its nest in holes in trees or dead snags or under or in artificial structures like fence posts and the eaves of buildings. The white-rumped swallow is solitary and nests in distributed pairs during the breeding season. The breeding season is from October to December in Brazil and from October to February in neighboring Argentina. Usually, only one brood with four to seven eggs is laid, although a second one will occasionally be laid. The female incubates the eggs over a period usually between 15 and 16 days, with the fledging usually occurring between 21 and 25 days after hatching.

children.name: Tachycineta euchrysea
children.description: The golden swallow (Tachycineta euchrysea) is a swallow endemic to the Caribbean island of Hispaniola (split between the Dominican Republic and Haiti) and was once native to Jamaica, but is now extirpated there.

children.name: Tachycineta albilinea
children.description: ]] The mangrove swallow (Tachycineta albilinea) is a passerine bird in the swallow family that breeds in coastal regions from Mexico through Central America to Panama.

children.name: Stelgidopteryx
children.description: Rough-winged swallows — a New World genus of two species named for the tiny hook-like serrations on the outer primary feathers of the males. They are dull brown swallows without the iridescent plumage of many relatives, but are widespread and common in a variety of open habitats throughout the Americas. They nest in burrows and crevices in earth banks, often using old kingfisher holes.

children.name: Stelgidopteryx serripennis
children.description: The northern rough-winged swallow (Stelgidopteryx serripennis) is a small, migratory swallow.

children.name: Stelgidopteryx ruficollis
children.description: The southern rough-winged swallow (Stelgidopteryx ruficollis) a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Cheramoeca
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the white-backed swallow, one of Australia's most distinctively patterned hirundines. The genus is characterised by a unique combination of features including a deeply forked tail, white back, and pied plumage. The white-backed swallow occupies arid and semi-arid Australia, nesting in burrows it excavates in sandy soil.

children.name: Cheramoeca leucosterna
children.description: The white-backed swallow (Cheramoeca leucosterna) is a member of the swallow family Hirundinidae and is endemic to Australia. It is the only species placed in the genus Cheramoeca. As with all swallows, it is characterised by adaptation to aerial feeding. It can be identified by its white back, surrounded by black wings and tail. It has a wide distribution, from the southern part of the Australian continent, up to the Tropic of Capricorn. The white-backed swallow prefers grasslands and will create a burrow nest.

children.name: Alopochelidon
children.description: A monotypic genus comprising the tawny-headed swallow of South America. The genus has sometimes been placed within Stelgidopteryx but morphological and molecular data support its recognition as a distinct genus. The tawny-headed swallow is a bird of open woodland and savanna in central South America.

children.name: Alopochelidon fucata
children.description: The tawny-headed swallow (Alopochelidon fucata) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae. It is the only species placed in the genus Alopochelidon. It is found in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Falkland Islands, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela, where its natural habitats are dry savanna and subtropical or tropical seasonally wet or flooded lowland grassland.

children.name: Atticora
children.description: A genus of two elegant Amazonian swallows with distinctive banded or jet-black plumage. Atticora swallows are associated with major Amazonian rivers and their tributaries. They nest colonially in sandy riverbanks and are among the more distinctive hirundines of the Amazon basin.

children.name: Atticora fasciata
children.description:
The white-banded swallow (Atticora fasciata) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae. It is black with white thighs, a white breast, and has white bars on the edges of its wings. It has a distinct, deeply forked tail.
It is found in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, French Guiana, Guyana, Peru, Suriname, and Venezuela, in tropical lowlands. It is non-migratory. Its natural habitats are rivers and forested areas. It nests in burrows and does not use artificial cavities.

children.name: Atticora andecola
children.description: A high-altitude swallow of the open Andean puna, found from Peru south to northwestern Argentina and Chile at elevations typically above 3,500 m. It is the least typical Atticora, with plain brown upperparts and pale underparts, and was formerly placed in its own genus Haplochelidon. The species nests in burrows in earthen banks and is locally migratory in the non-breeding season.

children.name: Neochelidon
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the white-thighed swallow of northern South America, sometimes placed in Atticora. It is a small, dark swallow of forest edge and open country in lowland Amazonia and adjacent areas, identified by its white thigh tufts visible in flight.

children.name: Pygochelidon
children.description: A genus of two Andean and southern South American swallows formerly placed in Notiochelidon. They are small, blue-black swallows of open Andean habitats and Patagonian grasslands, often nesting in towns and villages at high altitude.

children.name: Pygochelidon cyanoleuca
children.description: The blue-and-white swallow (Pygochelidon cyanoleuca) is a passerine bird that breeds from Nicaragua south throughout South America, except in the deserts and the Amazon Basin. The southern race is migratory, wintering as far north as Trinidad, where it is a regular visitor. The nominate northern race may have bred on that island.

children.name: Pygochelidon patagonica
children.description: A recently separated species, formerly treated as the migratory subspecies of the blue-and-white swallow, breeding in Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego. It is a long-distance austral migrant, wintering as far north as Bolivia and Brazil. The species inhabits open Patagonian steppe and grassland near water.

children.name: Orochelidon
children.description: Andean martins — a genus of two high-altitude swallows of the Andes formerly placed in Notiochelidon. They inhabit open Andean puna and grassland, often at elevations above 3,000 m. Both are dark swallows with pale underparts and are typical aerial feeders of the open Andean sky.

children.name: Orochelidon murina
children.description: The brown-bellied swallow (Orochelidon murina) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins. It is found in Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela.

children.name: Orochelidon flavipes
children.description:
The pale-footed swallow (Orochelidon flavipes) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae. It is found in the northern Andes, from Venezuela to Bolivia. It is monotypic.
Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical moist montane forests. They are usually seen in small flocks, occasionally with the blue-and-white swallow.

children.name: Pseudochelidon
children.description: River martins — a primitive genus of two highly distinctive swallows placed in their own subfamily, Pseudochelidoninae, owing to their aberrant morphology: they have large eyes, heavy bills, stout legs, and rounded wings unlike any other hirundine. The African river martin breeds on sandbars in the Congo River, while the white-eyed river martin was last confirmed on its Thai wintering grounds in the 1970s and may be extinct.

children.name: Pseudochelidon eurystomina
children.description:
The African river martin (Pseudochelidon eurystomina) is a passerine bird, one of two members of the river martin subfamily of the swallow family, Hirundinidae. When discovered, it was not initially recognised as a swallow, and its structural differences from most of its relatives, including its stout bill and robust legs and feet, have led to its current placement in a separate subfamily shared only with the Asian white-eyed river martin. The African river martin is a large swallow, mainly black with a blue-green gloss to the head and a greener tint to the back and wings. The under-wings are brownish, the underparts are purple-black, and the flight feathers are black. This martin has red eyes, a broad orange-red bill and a black, square tail. Young birds are similar in appearance to the adults, but have browner plumage. This species has a variety of unmusical calls, and displays both in flight and on the ground, although the purpose of the terrestrial display is unknown.
The main breeding areas are in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) along the Congo River and its tributary, the Ubangi, in habitats characterised by a mixture of tropical forest types including swampy or seasonally flooded woodland. The African river martin is migratory, wintering in coastal savanna in southern Gabon and the Republic of the Congo. Breeding also occurs in these coastal areas, but it is unknown whether the migrants are raising a second brood or if there is a separate resident population. This martin feeds in flocks throughout the year, catching a variety of insects in the air, especially flying ants. It does not use perches during the breeding season, although it will often land on the ground.

children.name: Pseudochelidon sirintarae
children.description:
The white-eyed river martin (Pseudochelidon sirintarae) is a passerine bird, one of only two members of the river martin subfamily of the swallows. Since it has significant differences from its closest relative, the African river martin, it is sometimes placed in its own genus, Eurochelidon. First found in 1968, it is known only from a single wintering site in Thailand, and may be extinct, since it has not been seen since 1980 despite targeted surveys in Thailand and neighbouring Cambodia. It may possibly still breed in China or Southeast Asia, but a Chinese painting initially thought to depict this species was later reassessed as showing pratincoles.
The adult white-eyed river martin is a medium-sized swallow, with mainly glossy greenish-black plumage, a white rump, and a tail which has two elongated slender central tail feathers, each widening to a racket-shape at the tip. It has a white eye ring and a broad, bright greenish-yellow bill. The sexes are similar in appearance, but the juvenile lacks the tail ornaments and is generally browner than the adult. Little is known of the behaviour or breeding habitat of this martin, although like other swallows it feeds on insects caught in flight, and its wide bill suggests that it may take relatively large species. It roosts in reed beds in winter, and may nest in river sandbanks, probably in April or May before the summer rains. It may have been overlooked prior to its discovery because it tended to feed at dawn or dusk rather than during the day.
